body_markdown:
The Goodwood Revival is famous for its thrilling historic racing, commitment to period-correct everything, and, of course, the outfits. But there’s an auction attached to the event, too. Typically, it’s a mix of postwar sports cars and racing machinery, along with other miscellaneous classics and some automobilia thrown in, but this year there was also a contingent of weird and wonderful stuff that was impossible to ignore. These included lots of early ’60s Japanese stuff you almost never see, as well as some unusual British stuff you almost never see, either. Almost all of them sold for cheap, too. Here they are, below.


## 1966 Mazda P360 Carol


Bonhams


Bonhams


Bonhams


**Sold for[£8050](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/208/c1966-mazda-p360-carol-saloon-chassis-no-kpda-250923-engine-no-da-1616/) ($10,764)**


Mazda only released its first car in 1960, so this is an early little piece or the Hiroshima company’s history. Built to Japan’s kei car class that limits size and engine capacity, the “Carol” came with an itty-bitty 358-cc four-cylinder and four-speed gearbox mounted in back.


Notable for its unibody construction, torsion bar suspension, and for having one of the smallest four-bangers ever dropped in an automobile, the Carol was a sales success in its home market, with more than a quarter-million copies sold, though they’re an uncommon sight outside of Japan. It looks like a shrunken Ford Anglia 105E or Citroën Ami 6.


## 1965 Toyota Publica 700 DX


Bonhams


**Sold for[£4830](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/205/c1965-toyota-publica-700-dx-saloon-chassis-no-4-up10-100568-engine-no-u96377/)** **($6459)**


When the Japanese Ministry of International Trade and Industry formulated its “national car” concept for the 1960s, it included requirements like a 100 km/h speed, 400 kg maximum weight, fuel efficiency of 71 mpg, and the ability to go at least 100,000 km without breakdowns or significant repairs. It was a tall order 60-plus years ago, but Toyota stepped up with the Publica in 1961. The front-mounted, air-cooled boxer twin displaced 697 cc and drove the rear wheels. Toyota developed the model over three series and offered it in multiple body styles until 1978. This one is a standard two-door sedan.


## 1969 Mitsubishi 500


Bonhams


**Sold for[£3450](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/217/1969-mitsubishi-500-saloon-chassis-no-60-a10-01688-engine-no-ne19a-02020/)** **($4613)**


After the Second World War, Mitsubishi was broken up into smaller entities, and there wasn’t a proper car wearing the three-diamond badge until the original Mitsubishi 500 arrived at the dawn of the 1960s. Under that bulbous body is unibody construction, a 594-cc air-cooled four-stroke twin at the rear, along with a three-speed manual. This one was reportedly restored in the late 1980s in a garden shed in Japan, but has been sitting since 1999.


## 1976 Suzuki Fronte Coupe


Bonhams


**Sold for[£8050](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/212/c1976-suzuki-fronte-coupe-chassis-no-lc10w-323272/)** **($10,764)**


Essentially a sedan version of Suzuki’s “Suzulight” van, the Fronte came out in 1962. Initial versions came with a two-stroke twin driving the front wheels, and the model was built to Japan’s kei car dimensions. The model proved popular with Japanese urbanites, and in 1970 the third-gen Fronte came out. With ’70s creases and angles, it earned the nickname “Sting Ray” but otherwise has almost nothing in common with America’s sports car. The engine was still a two-stroke twin, though a water-cooled version came out in 1971. This example is one of the later Fronte coupes, penned by Giorgetto Giugiaro and powered by a three-cylinder two-stroke. Another, slightly more conventional looking 1969 Fronte sold for[£4,830](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/216/c1969-suzuki-fronte-360-deluxe-microcar-chassis-no-lc10-183605/) out of the same collection.


## 1925 Lanchester 40hp Skiff


Bonhams


Bonhams


Bonhams


**Sold for[£92,000](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/241/1925-lanchester-40hp-skiff-chassis-no-1967-engine-no-1962/)** **($123,022)**


Lanchester is an obscure name today, but the carmaker founded by three brothers in the late 19th century was one of Britain’s most innovative during the early 20th. Lanchester experimented with and/or marketed disc brakes, turbocharging, the accelerator pedal, detachable wire wheels and fuel injection, all before 1910. Their later 40hp model was a high-end six-cylinder motorcar popular with the rich, famous, and royal, as well as with racers. It’s unclear when this one got its boat-inspired skiff bodywork, but it is made of Burmese teak and English ash.


It wasn’t the only home-grown British skiff in this sale, either, as a 1922 Rolls-Royce 40/50hp Silver Ghost sold later in the day for[£69,000](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/267/1922-rolls-royce-4050hp-silver-ghost-boat-tail-tourer-chassis-no-41sg/) ($92,267)


## 1982 Jaguar 4.2-Liter Owen Sedanca Coupe


Bonhams


**Sold for[£18,400](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31857/lot/252/1982-jaguar-42-litre-owen-sedanca-coupe-chassis-no-28749-engine-no-7j1549255/)** **($24,604)**


London car dealership H.R. Owen is nearly 100 years old, still running, and still focused on the high-end stuff just as it was when it started as a Rolls-Royce/Bentley store in 1932. In the early 1970s, it even commissioned this sharp “Sedanca,” a Lamborghini Espada–inspired aluminum hatchback based on Jaguar XJ6 underpinnings. North London coachbuilder Williams & Pritchard built the body, and although H.R. Owen quoted it as more than double the cost of a standard XJ6, the dealership secured 80 orders at the London Motor Show in September 1973.


Bonhams


Bonhams


Unfortunately, in October 1973, the oil crisis kicked off and reportedly every single order got canceled. After two prototypes were completed, two more were built in the late 1970s and early 1980s. This example is one of the later creations, though the Jaguar underneath is a 1972 model.
